question.problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,0,-2)?$

current_example.problem: In what direction does the function $f (x, y) = \ln (x^2y)$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(2, 1)?$
current_example.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-\nabla f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}y))\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}y))\text{ }j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\cdot 2xy\text{ }i-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\cdot {x}^{2}j \\  & =-\frac{2}{x}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j \\ -∇f(2,1) & =-\frac{2}{2}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{1}\text{ }j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $- \, \mathbf i - \mathbf j.$
